content: A nocturnal emission refers to the involuntary ejaculation of semen that occurs during sleep in males. This phenomenon is also commonly known as a wet dream or an involuntary orgasm during sleep. It is most frequently observed during adolescence and early adulthood, although it can occur at any point after puberty. Nocturnal emissions may or may not be accompanied by erotic dreams, and the ejaculation can happen even in the absence of an erection. Some individuals may wake up during the event, while others may remain asleep throughout the process, often referred to as a sex dream. It is important to note that women can also experience orgasms during sleep. The frequency of nocturnal emissions varies significantly among individuals. Some men report experiencing numerous nocturnal emissions during their teenage years, while others may never experience one. Studies indicate that approximately 83% of men in the United States will experience a nocturnal emission at some point in their lives. In cultures where masturbation is culturally discouraged, surveys show that over 98% of men eventually experience nocturnal emissions. The frequency of these events is not conclusively linked to the frequency of masturbation. Alfred Kinsey, a prominent sex researcher, observed that men with higher frequencies of nocturnal emissions might have slightly lower rates of masturbation, though the causality of this relationship remains unclear. For women, the correlation between sleep orgasms and other sexual activities is similarly inconclusive. Kinsey's research found that women who lost the opportunity for frequent coital orgasms experienced only a slight increase in sleep orgasms annually. Testosterone levels can influence the occurrence of nocturnal emissions. A 1998 study demonstrated that increasing testosterone doses in boys led to a significant rise in the number of reported nocturnal emissions, from 17% in untreated subjects to 90% in those receiving high doses. During puberty, 13% of males experience their first ejaculation as a result of a nocturnal emission. Kinsey also noted that males whose first ejaculation occurred through a nocturnal emission were generally older than those whose first ejaculation resulted from masturbation. This delay in first ejaculation through nocturnal emissions was estimated to be about a year or more compared to what would have been developmentally possible through physical stimulation. Unlike typical ejaculations, which usually terminate an erection, nocturnal emissions often leave the individual with a functional erection afterward. While various treatments claim to prevent or reduce nocturnal emissions, none have undergone rigorous scientific validation or approval processes, such as those required by the Food and Drug Administration. Many purported remedies lack a scientific basis and are comparable to unproven home remedies. Since nocturnal emissions do not cause physical harm beyond the inconvenience of cleaning up and are not indicative of any underlying medical condition, treatment is generally considered unnecessary. In rare cases, involuntary orgasms can occur during waking hours in both sexes. Regarding women, a 1953 study by Kinsey found that 40% of women experienced at least one orgasm during sleep by the age of 45. A 1986 study published in the Journal of Sex Research reported that 85% of women who experienced sleep orgasms first did so at a young age, often before the age of 21, and in some cases, before the age of 13. Historically, in the 18th and 19th centuries, frequent involuntary orgasms or excessive semen release were diagnosed as a condition called spermatorrhea or seminal weakness. Treatments for this supposed condition included drugs, circumcision, and even castration. While some modern practitioners, particularly herbalists, continue to diagnose and treat spermatorrhea, these treatments lack validation through rigorous experimentation. Religious perspectives on nocturnal emissions have varied. Saint Augustine argued that nocturnal emissions, unlike masturbation, did not corrupt a man's conscience because they were involuntary and not deliberate carnal acts, and thus were not considered sinful. However, Augustine prayed for deliverance from the glue of lust and recommended seeking divine assistance to cleanse one's soul of carnal desires. Certain parts of the Bible indirectly reference nocturnal emissions, using the Hebrew term tameh, often translated as impure. For example, the resulting impurity required ritual bathing in a mikveh. Even a man who had normal intercourse with his wife was considered ceremonially unclean and required to bathe in a mikveh, becoming pure after sunset. Similar statements are made in Leviticus regarding menstruation and childbirth. Psalms are still recited on Yom Kippur at night as a supposed aid against nocturnal emissions, particularly because bathing is forbidden on that day. In medieval Western occultism, nocturnal emissions were sometimes attributed to encounters with a succubus, a mythical being believed to engage in sexual activity with individuals during sleep. This belief was often associated with night terrors.
